paragraphs.source_en: What happened to the hunter-gatherers in the Central Sahara with the onset of desert conditions from around 3,000 BP? There is not enough archaeological data to reconstruct the exact situation but two main hypotheses may be advanced. After a presumed long coexistence of hunters and pastoralists in the same region, it is plausible that at least some of the hunters also adopted the productive economy based on domesticated cattle and goats. A similar situation is known from a recent period in South Africa where some of the San hunters gradually adopted the lifestyle of their sedentary farmer neighbours (Lee 1979).

units.source_en: There is not enough archaeological data to reconstruct the exact situation but two main hypotheses may be advanced.

After a presumed long coexistence of hunters and pastoralists in the same region, it is plausible that at least some of the hunters also adopted the productive economy based on domesticated cattle and goats.
A similar situation is known from a recent period in South Africa where some of the San hunters gradually adopted the lifestyle of their sedentary farmer neighbours (Lee 1979).

paragraphs.source_en: The pastoral economy in the Central Sahara was clearly the predominant kind of subsistence in the increasingly arid environment, which is also attested to archaeologically (Barich 1998a; Cremaschi & Di Lernia 2001). Cattle herding has continued since 7,500 BP until very recently in the Sahara and until today in the Sahel. The success of pastoralism is further confirmed by its enormous spread over a large area covering a great part of North Africa. There is no reason to suppose that all groups of hunters would keep their way of life in the proximity of the successful pastoral economy. Can a possible adoption of domesticates be observed in the Round Head rock art? There are no scenes of domestication in this artistic complex, however, some indicators may suggest a possible change.

paragraphs.source_en: At Uan Mata in the Tassili, there are two outstanding paintings of cattle. Their horns are curved in two different ways but both are typical for domesticated cattle. Whereas only the head with its upwards curved long horns is visible on the first animal, the second animal is well preserved (Fig. 4-7). Its horns are large and curved in the shape of a lyre and between its back legs a probable udder is represented. The style of these animals is uncertain, however the typical thick red border and white filling it evokes the Round Heads. These animals could be an example of domesticated cattle depicted by the creators of the Round Head art because they are painted near to other cattle of the Pastoral style.
